name: journal-paul-onesimus-and-slavery.json
content:
Paul sent a slave back to his master. The letter is short, polite and affectionate, and it never contains the word "free". That one fact answers most of what Christians say about Paul and slavery.

The letter

Philemon is the shortest of Paul's letters and the only one about a single slave. Onesimus, a slave of Philemon, had come to Paul in prison, and Paul "became his father" there.1 Readers usually take Onesimus for a runaway. The letter never says so. It speaks of him being "parted" from Philemon and of wrongs and debts to be charged to Paul's account.2

Whatever the cause, Paul did not keep him. "I am sending him back to you, sending my very heart."3 A runaway slave in the Roman world could be beaten, branded or killed. Paul knew that, and he returned him to the man with the power to do it.

He asks Philemon to receive him "no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother".4 The sentence is warm. It also asks for a change of attitude, not a change of status.

[paulus_figure name="bundle-of-old-letters-envelopes-18690578"]A bundle of old letters. Philemon is a short private letter, and Paul uses it to return a slave to his owner.[/paulus_figure]

What he left unsaid

Paul had leverage. He was Philemon's spiritual father, and he writes that he is "bold enough in Christ to command you to do what is required", and chooses to appeal instead.5 He says he "preferred to do nothing without your consent in order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord".6 Near the end comes a hint: "Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say."7

That is as close as the letter comes. Some readers take "even more than I say" as a request to free Onesimus. Paul could have written the request in one word, and he did not. The institution stands untouched. A slave owner who finishes the letter can free his slave or keep him, and Paul has left both doors open.

The debt he mentions

Paul does not appeal on kindness alone. He offers to pay whatever Onesimus owes, and then reminds Philemon of what he owes in return: "I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it—to say nothing of your owing me even your own self."8 The pressure is plain. Philemon is in Paul's debt for his own conversion, and Paul says so in the same breath as he offers to settle the account.

A man who uses that much leverage and still stops short of asking for the slave's freedom has made a choice. The leverage was available and the request was left out.

Neither slave nor free

The silence stands out against what Paul wrote elsewhere. To the Galatians he says that in Christ "there is neither slave nor free".9 The line is quoted often. Philemon is the one place where Paul had a real slave and a real owner in front of him, and the line did no work. The principle was for sermons. The letter was for the owner.

Stay as you were called

Paul's advice to slaves in 1 Corinthians points the same way. "Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called." Then: "Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.)"10 The Greek of the second sentence is short, and translators divide on whether Paul recommends freedom or tells the slave to make the most of slavery. Even on the kinder reading, freedom is an option for the lucky. The rule is to stay put.

The letters in his name

The later letters that carry Paul's name speak plainly. "Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters", says Colossians.11 Ephesians adds "with fear and trembling".12 Titus says slaves are "to be submissive to their own masters in everything",13 and 1 Timothy says they should "regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled".14

This site treats those four letters as the work of Paul's school. The instructions still came out of the movement he founded, and they fit the one letter he wrote himself. [paulus_link slug="women-slaves-and-caesar" /] sets out the whole pattern: women told to be silent, slaves told to obey and subjects told to submit to Caesar.

A Muslim reading

The Qurʾān puts the freeing of a slave among the acts of righteousness (Sūrah al-Balad 90:13), prescribes it as atonement (al-Nisāʾ 4:92) and provides a way for a slave to contract for his own freedom (al-Nūr 24:33). Paul had a slave and an owner in front of him and wrote a letter that asks for a kind word.

The verdict

A man who wrote that in Christ there is neither slave nor free sent a slave back to his owner and asked politely for kindness. He never wrote the word "freedom". His own advice to slaves is to stay as they are, and the letters under his name tell them to obey.

For centuries slaveholding Christians read those lines as permission, and they had no trouble finding it. Paul gave it by saying nothing against the institution and a good deal for obedience. [paulus_link slug="the-flesh" /] shows the same pattern in what he said about the body.

Paul and slavery: questions readers ask

Did Paul free Onesimus?

No. He sent Onesimus back to his owner, Philemon, and asked him to receive him as a brother. The letter never asks for his freedom in so many words.

Did Paul condemn slavery?

No letter condemns it. Philemon, 1 Corinthians 7 and the letters in his name all take the institution for granted and give instructions inside it.

What does 1 Corinthians 7:21 mean?

Paul tells slaves not to be concerned about their condition, and adds that they should take freedom if it is offered. The Greek is ambiguous, and some translators read the second half as advice to stay a slave.

Who wrote the letters that tell slaves to obey?

Colossians, Ephesians, Titus and 1 Timothy carry Paul's name. This site treats all four as written by his followers, though the instruction fits what Paul himself wrote in Philemon and 1 Corinthians.
